task: Research the components of fitness and the principles of training, then design a six week training plan with goals to improve your performance in a sport of your choice. Explain and justify your plan.
text:
Training plan: improving my 5 km cross-country time

1. Why I chose this and where I am now

I run for the school cross-country team and in the district race in October I finished the 5 km course in 27:40, which put me 14th out of 31 in my age group. My coach said my pace at the start was fine but I lost a lot of places in the last kilometre. That tells me my main limiter is not speed but aerobic endurance, and probably also how well my legs cope with fatigue. To check this I did two tests before planning. The first was the 12 minute Cooper run, where I covered 2,350 m. For a 15 year old boy that is about average, which is not good enough if I want to finish in the top third. The second was a resting heart rate check for three mornings, which averaged 68 beats per minute. A fit teenage endurance runner is often lower than this, so my heart is not yet as efficient as it could be at pumping blood.

2. Components of fitness and how they matter for 5 km running

Fitness is made up of health related components and skill related components. For a 5 km run the most important health related component is cardiovascular (aerobic) endurance, which is the ability of the heart, lungs and blood vessels to deliver oxygen to working muscles for a long time. A 5 km race takes me about 27 minutes, so most of the energy comes from the aerobic energy system, where glucose and fat are broken down with oxygen. The anaerobic system (without oxygen) produces lactate and is only really important at the start and in the final sprint, which is why a person who trains only sprints will still struggle in a 5 km. The second component is muscular endurance, because my quadriceps, calves and hamstrings must contract thousands of times without tiring. Flexibility matters less but a tight hip or calf shortens my stride and raises injury risk. From the skill related components, I think the most relevant are power (for hills) and balance (for uneven grass), but I will not directly test them in this plan.

I also learned that the body adapts when stress is applied. Regular aerobic training increases stroke volume (the amount of blood pumped per beat), the number of capillaries around muscle fibres and the number of mitochondria in muscle cells. This is why resting heart rate falls as a person becomes fitter, and why my resting heart rate of 68 is a good measure to track.

3. Principles of training I will apply

Specificity: training must match the demands of the sport, so most of my sessions will be running, not gym work. Progressive overload: I must gradually increase the workload so that the body keeps adapting, but I will follow the rule of increasing weekly distance by no more than about 10 percent to avoid shin splints or stress injuries, which I got in Year 8 when I increased too quickly. Individuality: my plan is based on my own test scores and my own school timetable, not on a plan copied from a professional runner. Reversibility: if I stop, fitness is lost, so I have to be consistent, and I have planned rest only as planned recovery. I will also use the FITT principle (frequency, intensity, time, type) to describe each session.

4. SMART goals

Main goal: To lower my 5 km time from 27:40 to 25:30 (a reduction of 2 min 10 s, about 8 percent) by the school time trial on Friday 15 November, six weeks from now.
Specific: 5 km time on the same school course.
Measurable: timed with a stopwatch by my PE teacher, same course, same conditions as far as possible.
Achievable: an 8 percent improvement in six weeks is realistic for a teenager who has not yet followed a structured plan; my coach agrees.
Relevant: it is the distance that I race in the team.
Time-bound: the date of the trial.

Supporting goals: (a) increase the Cooper test distance from 2,350 m to 2,550 m by week 6; (b) reduce resting heart rate from 68 to 64 bpm; (c) complete at least 17 of the 18 planned sessions to make sure that the plan is followed.

5. The plan

Week 1: Mon 25 min easy run (heart rate zone 2), Wed 20 min easy run + 4 x 20 s strides, Sat 35 min long steady run. Total about 14 km.
Week 2: same pattern, Saturday run 40 min. About 15 km.
Week 3: Mon 30 min easy, Wed intervals 5 x 3 min at 5 km race effort with 90 s jog recovery, Sat 40 min. About 16 km.
Week 4 (recovery week): Mon 25 min easy, Wed 5 x 2 min intervals, Sat 30 min easy. About 12 km.
Week 5: Mon 30 min easy, Wed 6 x 3 min intervals with 90 s recovery, Sat 45 min long run. About 17 km.
Week 6 (taper): Mon 25 min easy, Wed 3 x 3 min at race pace, Sat rest, then the time trial on Friday.
Every Tuesday and Thursday I will do 15 minutes of core and leg strength (squats, lunges, calf raises, planks) as muscular endurance work. Every session begins with 8 minutes of dynamic warm-up and ends with 5 minutes of jogging and static stretching.

6. Justification

Two thirds of my sessions are easy running at conversational pace because aerobic base building is what improves stroke volume and capillary density. I chose intervals once a week from week 3 because interval training at about race pace raises my VO2 max and teaches me to tolerate lactate, but I do not start them in weeks 1 and 2 because my body needs to get used to the extra volume first (progressive overload). Week 4 has less distance because adaptations actually happen during recovery, and a down week every third or fourth week lowers the risk of overuse injury. The taper in week 6 reduces volume but keeps some intensity so that my legs are fresh for the time trial. The strength work is short so that it does not tire my legs for running.

7. Monitoring and safety

I will keep a training log (distance, time, how I felt out of 10, resting heart rate) and repeat the Cooper test at the end of week 3 to see if I am on track. If my resting heart rate is more than 5 beats higher than usual or I feel sharp pain, I will swap the session for rest. I will drink water before sessions, eat carbohydrates such as pasta or rice the evening before long runs and wear proper running shoes, as the old ones I own have worn soles. Because I may run in the evenings when it gets dark, I will wear reflective clothing and run on the school track or with my brother.

task: Research the components of fitness and the principles of training, then design a six week training plan with goals to improve your performance in a sport of your choice. Explain and justify your plan.
text:
My badminton training plan

Introduction

I play badminton at school and also at a club on Saturdays. Badminton is a fast racket sport that is played in singles and doubles. You have to hit a shuttlecock over the net and the aim is to make it land on the floor on the other side. A game goes up to 21 points and you win a match by winning two games. I like badminton because it is exciting and you have to think fast. In this task I will talk about fitness and make a plan to get better at badminton.

Components of fitness

There are different components of fitness and they are all important for sport. The health related ones are cardiovascular endurance, muscular endurance, muscular strength, flexibility and body composition. The skill related ones are agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time and speed. In badminton I think most of these are used. Agility is important because you have to change direction quickly to get to the shuttle. Reaction time is important because smashes come very fast, sometimes over 200 km per hour. Power is used for smashing and jumping. Flexibility helps you reach for the shuttle and stops you from getting injured. Cardiovascular endurance means that the heart and lungs can give the muscles oxygen for a long time so you do not get tired in a long match. Muscular strength means how hard the muscles can push or pull. When I play a long game I get tired in the third game, and my legs feel heavy, so I think I need to improve endurance and also my leg strength. I also think my smash is quite weak.

Energy systems are another thing. In badminton the body uses the aerobic system and the anaerobic system. Aerobic needs oxygen and anaerobic does not. When you work hard without enough oxygen your muscles make lactic acid, and this makes your muscles hurt, and that is why you get cramps. Rallies in badminton are short so the body uses the anaerobic system for them and then aerobic for recovery between points.

Principles of training

There are principles of training. These are FITT which means frequency, intensity, time and type. Overload is when you work harder than normal so you improve. Progression means you make it a bit harder each week. Specificity means that training must be like your sport. Reversibility means you lose fitness if you stop. I will use these in my plan.

Goals

My goals are to get fitter, improve my smash and get better at playing badminton. I also want to win more matches at the club and to be better at moving around the court. I would like to improve my fitness by the end of the plan and feel less tired in matches. I want to be a better player overall.

My plan

The plan is for six weeks and I will train four days a week.

Monday: run for 20 minutes and do skipping for 5 minutes.
Tuesday: shadow badminton footwork for 20 minutes, 3 sets of 10 lunges, 3 sets of 10 squats.
Thursday: practice smashes with a partner for 30 minutes, then do some stretches.
Saturday: club session where I play games for 90 minutes.
Sunday: rest.

In weeks 3 and 4 I will run for 25 minutes and do 3 sets of 12 lunges and squats. In weeks 5 and 6 I will run for 30 minutes and do 4 sets of 12 lunges and squats and do smashes for 40 minutes. Every session I will do a warm up first, for example jogging and arm circles, and a cool down at the end.

Why I chose these exercises

I chose running because it improves cardiovascular endurance, which I need so that I do not get tired. I chose skipping because it is good for footwork and it is also cardio. Lunges and squats strengthen the legs, which are used a lot in badminton when you lunge to the net. Smash practice will improve my smash. I chose the club session because it is good to play real games.

Safety

To make sure I do not get injured I will warm up and cool down, wear good shoes and drink water. I will also not train when I am ill. If I feel pain I will stop.

How I will check progress

At the end of the six weeks I will see if I feel fitter and if I win more matches. I will also ask my coach if my smash is better. If the plan is working I will carry on with it and if it is not working I will change it.

Conclusion

In conclusion I think this plan will help me to improve my badminton because it has cardio, strength and skill practice. Badminton is a great sport and I really enjoy it, so I think I will stick to the plan and do my best. I think that by the end of the six weeks I will be a better badminton player.

task: Research the components of fitness and the principles of training, then design a six week training plan with goals to improve your performance in a sport of your choice. Explain and justify your plan.
text:
Training plan for football

I play football for my school team and I play in midfield. I want to be better at football so I am going to make a training plan.

Fitness is when you are healthy and can do sport without getting tired. There are lots of parts of fitness like stamina, strength, speed and flexibility. Stamina is how long you can run for and strength is how strong you are. Speed is how fast you are and flexibility is when you can stretch. In football you need all of them because you run a lot in a game and you need to kick the ball hard. Football players also have to eat healthy food and drink water.

The FITT principle is something we learnt in class. It is Frequency, Intensity, Time and Type. Frequency is how often you train, Intensity is how hard, Time is how long and Type is what kind of exercise. I will use FITT to help me.

My goals are to get fitter and run faster. I also want to score more goals and to be good at passing.

My plan is:

Monday - run around the field
Tuesday - football practice at school
Wednesday - rest
Thursday - do some sprints and press ups
Friday - football practice at school
Saturday - play a match
Sunday - rest

I will do this for six weeks. I will run for longer each week so I get fitter. In the first week I will run for 10 minutes and then in week two I will run for 15 minutes and so on. I will do sprints because football players need to be fast. Press ups are good for my strength.

I will warm up before I do sport so that I do not get hurt. The warm up is jogging and stretching. After the exercise I will cool down.

I think this plan will work because I will train lots and I will get better at football. If I do the training I will be fitter and play better in the matches. At the end I will see if I am fitter and if I am not then I will try harder.

task: Write a reflection on your basketball unit. Evaluate how well you showed interpersonal skills, how effective your training plan was, and how well you performed. Say what you would change to improve your performance.
text:
Reflection: basketball unit

Interpersonal skills

At the start of the unit I thought my communication was one of my strengths because I talk a lot on the court. After watching the video our teacher filmed in week 3, I changed my mind. Most of what I said was shouting for the ball or complaining ("pass it!"), and almost none of it helped my teammates. In the first game against 9C I turned the ball over four times because I forced passes to Daniel when he was marked, and then I told him off in front of everyone. His reaction was to stop moving to get open, which hurt us more. My teacher pointed out that my tone was affecting the team's performance, so I set myself a target to give one positive or useful call each possession, such as "screen left" or "good look".

From week 4 I worked on this on purpose. I asked our quietest player, Priya, what calls helped her, and she said that she liked to be told where the free player was. I started calling out who was open before passing, and I also agreed with the team a simple signal for our zone press. In the final tournament match I counted eleven positive calls in the first half in my own notes, compared with maybe two in week 3. The video shows that Daniel and Priya received the ball more often and that we only lost the ball six times in the match, down from fourteen in the first game. I think this shows that better communication caused better team performance, though I cannot be sure it is the only cause because the opponents in the final game were weaker than 9C. I still lost my patience in the second half when we were two points down and I said "come on!" harshly. My next step is to use a breathing pause on the bench and talk to my team at timeouts calmly.

Effectiveness of my training plan

My plan had two aims: raise my free throw percentage from 4/10 to 7/10 and improve my left-handed layup so that I could use it in games. I trained three times a week for five weeks. For free throws I did 20 shots after each session and recorded them. My results by week were 4/10, 5/10, 5/10, 7/10 and 6/10, and in the final test I scored 7/10, so I reached the goal on the test. In games, however, I only made 3 of 8 free throws, which tells me that my success under pressure is not the same as in practice. I think this happened because I practised alone and without tiredness or noise. In my plan I should have added shots after sprints and with classmates trying to distract me, which would be more specific to the game.

The left-hand layup drill was more successful. In week 1 I made 2 out of 10 from the left side and by week 5 I made 8 out of 10. In the final match I used the left-handed layup twice, and scored once, which would not have been possible at the start. The progression of the drill (stationary, then walking, then dribbling at speed, then with a defender) was effective because each step was a bit harder, and I only moved on when I made 7 out of 10. One weakness of my plan was fitness. I put in little conditioning, and by the last quarter of every match my shooting got worse and I got slower getting back on defence. My teacher noticed that. My fitness test (the beep test) went from level 7.2 to 7.4, so there was almost no change.

Performance

On the match performance sheet my teacher marked me on a scale of 1 to 5. My dribbling was a 4, passing a 3, shooting a 3 and defence a 2. The biggest weakness was defence. I often reached in for steals instead of moving my feet, which caused three fouls in the final game. In games I scored a total of 14 points over the 3 matches, with 5 assists, which was better than my starting level of 2 points and 0 assists in game 1. I would say that my performance improved mostly with offence and less with defence, because my plan did not include defence at all, which I now think was a poor decision.

What I would change

If I did this unit again I would change four things. First, I would include defensive footwork drills (defensive slides, closing out) twice a week because defence was my lowest score. Second, I would make my free throw practice more realistic by adding pressure. Third, I would add a 10 minute interval conditioning block, for example 30 seconds sprint and 30 seconds rest repeated eight times, to improve my endurance in the fourth quarter. Fourth, I would set a numerical target for communication, such as ten helpful calls per match, and ask a teammate to count them so that I do not rely on my own opinion. Overall I think I improved most where I measured and practised on purpose, and least where I did not plan at all.

task: Write a reflection on your basketball unit. Evaluate how well you showed interpersonal skills, how effective your training plan was, and how well you performed. Say what you would change to improve your performance.
text:
Basketball reflection

In this unit we played basketball for six weeks. We learned how to dribble, pass, shoot and play in a team, and at the end we played a tournament between the classes. I did a training plan to improve my shooting and fitness. In this reflection I will talk about my interpersonal skills, my plan and my performance and what I could improve.

Interpersonal skills

I think my interpersonal skills were good in this unit. I worked well with my team and we got along. I tried to encourage my teammates when they missed a shot by saying things like "good try" and "next time". I also passed the ball to others and not just kept it for myself. One time in the second game my teammate Ahmed was upset because he missed an easy shot, and I told him it was fine and we all make mistakes. I think this helped him because he scored in the next quarter. Sometimes I was a bit bossy and told people where to go, which some people didn't like, but I was trying to help the team win. I think teamwork is very important in basketball because you cannot win alone. We communicated by talking to each other during the game and this was a strength of our team. A weakness might be that we sometimes all talked at once. Next time I will listen more.

My training plan

My training plan was to get better at shooting and to improve my fitness. I trained on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays for 5 weeks. On Monday I practised free throws, on Wednesday I did layups and on Friday I ran laps and did skipping. At the start I could score about 3 out of 10 free throws and at the end of the plan I could score about 5 out of 10. So I improved by 2, which is good. My layups also got better and I could do them with my left hand a bit. I think the plan was effective because I practised a lot and my shooting improved. My fitness got better too and I wasn't as tired in the games as before. However I did miss two sessions because I was ill with a cold and one because I had a school trip, so I didn't do the whole plan. If I did all the sessions I think that I would have improved more.

The plan was good because it was specific to basketball and I enjoyed doing it. The skipping was good for my endurance. I did not really test my fitness at the end, but I felt fitter. One thing that was not so good was that I did not have a partner to train with so sometimes it was boring and hard to stay motivated.

My performance

In the tournament we played three matches. We won the first one, lost the second and drew the third. Overall I think I played quite well. I scored some points in each game and I did some good passes. My defence was OK, I tried to mark my opponent and I got one steal. I think my best skill was dribbling because I could dribble without looking at the ball. My worst skill was probably shooting from far away because I always missed it. I also sometimes travelled with the ball, which the teacher said was a mistake. My teacher gave me a 5 out of 8 for performance, which I think is fair. I was a bit nervous in the last match because there were people watching, but then I calmed down.

What I would do to improve

To improve I need to practise my shooting more. I also need to work on my defence and my fitness. Next time I will make a better plan and I will do it every week without missing sessions. I will also try to find someone to train with, perhaps my brother, because that would motivate me. I should also practise dribbling with my left hand since I mostly use my right. I will also try to be less bossy and be a better listener in the team. If I do these things I think I can be a lot better at basketball.

In conclusion, the unit was good and I learned a lot. I improved my shooting and I worked well in my team. I enjoyed the tournament because it was fun to play against other classes. I think I did well overall but there are some things I can do better next time. I would like to play basketball in a club in the future, so I will keep practising these skills at home and at the park.

Another thing I learned is about health. Playing sport is good for your body and your mind because it makes you happy and reduces stress. After basketball lessons I felt more focused in my other lessons. That is why I will keep on playing sport even after this unit has finished and encourage my friends to play with me.

task: Write a reflection on your basketball unit. Evaluate how well you showed interpersonal skills, how effective your training plan was, and how well you performed. Say what you would change to improve your performance.
text:
Reflection

In this unit we did basketball. It was fun and I liked it. I played with my team and we played some matches.

My interpersonal skills were good. I worked with my team and I was nice to everyone. I helped my team and we got on well. I think teamwork is important.

My training plan went well. I did the plan and I got better at basketball. I practised shooting and running. I think the plan worked because I was better at the end than at the start.

My performance was good. I played well in the matches and I scored some points. I did some good passes too. We won one game and lost one game. I think I did my best.

To improve I would try harder next time and practise more. I would also do more training and get fitter. I would try to be a better player and work with my team more.

Overall I think the unit went well and I learned some things. I want to do basketball again.

task: Complete your PHE unit portfolio on netball: (A) knowledge of fitness and skills, (B) your training plan with goals, (C) your performance in the unit, and (D) a reflection on your interpersonal skills, plan and performance.
text:
Netball portfolio

Note: this is my reflection on the netball unit. I did not write out the knowledge section or a full plan in this document.

Interpersonal skills

I played goal defence in the unit, which meant that I depended on my team all the time. In the first match I realised that I was not communicating well. Our goal keeper, Zara, and I both went for the same interception three times, and each time the other team got the ball. We had not agreed who was responsible for the circle edge. When I asked her afterwards, she said that she was afraid to call because I seemed to be annoyed when she did. I had not realised that my facial expressions showed frustration. So I decided to do two things: talk to Zara before each match about who covers which side, and say "mine" or "yours" loudly at the moment of the interception.

The effect was clear. In the last two matches we had no collisions in the circle, and the number of intercepts we made as a pair rose from 2 in the first match to 6 in the fourth, according to the stats sheet kept by the scorer. I also tried to listen to my captain, Mei, who was good at spotting where the other team was weak. When she told me to mark the shooter more tightly, I disagreed at first because I thought I was already close enough. But I tried it, and the shooter's accuracy fell, so I accepted that I had been wrong. I think my willingness to change my mind was a strength, but I was too slow to do it in the early weeks. In the future I will ask for feedback sooner, not after a mistake.

Effectiveness of what I did to prepare

I did not follow a structured training plan, so I cannot say that it was effective. I mostly practised my footwork and the defensive stance at lunchtime with a friend for about four sessions. I did not measure anything before or after, so I can only say that I felt quicker, and my teacher's comment that my footwork was better in week 5 is the only evidence. This is a clear weakness. If I did the unit again I would take a baseline, for example the number of successful intercepts in a drill, and set a target.

How I performed

I received a mix of feedback. Our teacher said my defensive positioning was good, but I was often penalised for contact, with 5 penalties in the second match and 2 in the last one. I think the improvement came from learning to keep my arms still and my feet moving rather than leaning into the shooter. My attacking passes from the defence were less accurate and I made several mistakes under pressure, perhaps because I was rushing. I think that I need to slow down and look for the centre court player before I pass. Our team won 2 of 4 matches and the final match was lost by only one goal, which made me feel that we were close to improving.

What I would change

First, I would write a real plan with numerical targets, for example 6 intercepts per match and fewer than 3 contact penalties. Second, I would practise passing under pressure with a defender, not alone against a wall. Third, I would speak up in the first match instead of waiting until after the third collision. Fourth, I would ask my teammates for feedback every second week, as this was the most useful thing I did in the unit and I only did it halfway through. Overall, I learned that to improve I need to measure what I do, not just feel that it went well.

task: Design folio part 1: identify a need and a client, research and analyse the need, existing products and a design brief (criterion A). Then write a specification, develop a range of feasible design ideas, choose and justify one design and show planning details (criterion B).
text:
DESIGN FOLIO
Library desk charging station
Year 10 MYP Design
Criterion A and B

SLIDE 2 - THE NEED
Problem: students at our school library charge phones and laptops at the long tables, but there are only 6 wall sockets for about 40 seats.
Cables lie across the tables, get tangled and get pulled off the edge.
Observed on Tuesday 4 March, 12:30-13:10: 9 students stood or crouched near sockets, 3 phones fell on the floor, 2 cables were pulled out when someone walked past.
Caption: photo of tangled cables at table 4 (taken with permission)

SLIDE 3 - CLIENT AND TARGET USER
Client: Mrs Okonkwo, school librarian.
Target users: students aged 11-18 who work in the library, about 120 per day.
Interview with client (4 March). Her points:
- "Cables are a trip risk and a fire safety worry."
- Wants something that is cheap enough to buy 6 of.
- Must not be screwed to the tables (tables are leased).
- Must be easy to wipe clean.
- Must fit the existing extension leads (the 4-way white type).

SLIDE 4 - RESEARCH PLAN
What I need to find out / how / why
1. How many devices students charge and what types - survey of 15 students - to decide the number of ports/slots.
2. What cable types and lengths students use - measure 10 cables - to size the cable channels.
3. What existing products do and where they fail - analyse 3 products - to find gaps.
4. Safety and material requirements - school safety rules, material properties - to choose a safe material.
5. Table size and layout - measure the library tables - to fix dimensions.
Sources: survey, interview, observation, measuring, online shops, school safety policy.

SLIDE 5 - SURVEY RESULTS (15 students, Year 7-12)
Q1 What do you charge in the library? phone 14, laptop 6, earbuds 5, tablet 2 (some chose more than one)
Q2 How many devices at once? 1 device: 6 students, 2 devices: 7 students, 3 devices: 2 students
Q3 What's the main problem? tangled cables 8, no free sockets 5, phone falls off the table 2
Q4 Would you use a station if available? yes 13, maybe 2
Conclusion: a station should hold a minimum of 3 devices, deal with tangling first, and keep phones off the floor.
Caption: bar chart of Q3 results

SLIDE 6 - MEASUREMENTS
Cable diameters: USB-C 3.5-4.5 mm, Lightning 3 mm, laptop charger 5-7 mm
Cable lengths: 1 m to 2 m
Phone thickness: 7-10 mm (with case up to 13 mm)
Laptop charger plug: 45 mm x 25 mm
Table: 180 cm x 75 cm, rounded edge, thickness 30 mm
Extension lead: 4-way, 33 cm long, 5 cm wide
So cable slots need to be 8 mm wide at least and the slot for a phone about 15 mm.

SLIDE 7 - ANALYSIS OF EXISTING PRODUCTS
Product 1: Cable clips (stick-on, silicone), 3 for 2.50 pounds
Pros: cheap, holds one cable each, easy to use
Cons: adhesive fails after weeks on laminate, no place for phone, only 1 cable each
Product 2: Charging dock for 4 phones (plastic), about 18 pounds
Pros: neat, holds phones upright, built-in cable guide
Cons: expensive, no space for laptops, has its own power so it adds a plug, fixed slot size does not fit thick cases
Product 3: Wooden desk organiser with cable hole, about 12 pounds
Pros: strong and good looking, replaceable
Cons: cable hole is small (6 mm) so chargers do not pass through, no space for lead, heavy 1.4 kg
Lesson: none of them combine holding a power strip, guiding multiple cables and supporting phones. Product 2 shows that upright holders are good, product 3 shows that a heavy base keeps things stable.

SLIDE 8 - SAFETY AND MATERIALS
School rule: no mains electrical item can be modified. So my product only holds the extension lead and does not alter it.
Materials considered: 6 mm plywood (cheap, laser cuttable, strong), acrylic (clean but cracks), PLA 3D print (accurate but slow, 8 hours)
Plywood sealed with varnish is wipeable. I will not cover vents on the lead.

SLIDE 9 - DESIGN BRIEF
Design and make a low cost desk charging station for the school library that holds a 4-way extension lead, keeps at least four cables organised and holds at least three phones upright, can be used without fixing to the table. The user is a student working at a long table and the client is the librarian. It must be safe and wipeable.

SLIDE 10 - SPECIFICATION (each point with how it will be tested)
1. Holds at least 3 phones upright (up to 13 mm thick) - test with 3 phones and cases
2. Has at least 4 cable slots, each at least 8 mm wide - measure
3. Holds a 33 x 5 cm lead securely; lead does not slide when I pull a cable with 5 N force - pull test with a spring balance
4. Footprint no bigger than 40 cm x 15 cm, height no more than 12 cm so it does not block the screen of a laptop - measure
5. Material cost under 8 pounds - receipts
6. Surface is smooth and sealed so it can be wiped - wipe test with damp cloth
7. No sharp edges - corners rounded, radius at least 3 mm, check by hand
8. Does not cover ventilation of the lead, and does not need to be fixed to the table - inspection
9. Can be made in 4 lessons with school laser cutter and hand tools

SLIDE 11 - IDEA 1: Tray with phone slots
Sketch: flat tray with 3 slanted slots along front, lead sits in the back
Annotations: slot 15 mm wide, angle 70 degrees, 6 mm ply
+ simple, cheap, stable
- cables tangle underneath, tray is long (40 cm)

SLIDE 12 - IDEA 2: Vertical tower
Sketch: tower 25 cm tall, lead mounted in base, phones hang on 3 arms
Annotations: base 15 x 15 cm
+ small footprint
- tips over easily, the arms break, blocks screen

SLIDE 13 - IDEA 3: Low box with lid channels
Sketch: box 38 x 12 x 8 cm, lead inside, 5 slots in the lid for cables, 3 phone slots at back edge
Annotations: lid slides off for the lead, cable slots 9 mm wide, rubber feet
+ hides lead and cable tangles, low centre of gravity, heavy base
- takes more cutting, more parts (6)

SLIDE 14 - IDEA 4: Clip-on edge organiser
Sketch: clips to the table edge, cable hooks
Annotations: needs the table edge 30 mm, plastic clamp
+ saves table space
- may mark leased tables, cable hooks not strong, no place for phones

SLIDE 15 - EVALUATING IDEAS (score 1-5, weight x)
Criteria / weight / Idea 1 / Idea 2 / Idea 3 / Idea 4
Stability (3): 4 / 2 / 5 / 3
Cable tidiness (3): 2 / 3 / 5 / 3
Phone holding (2): 4 / 3 / 4 / 1
Cost (2): 5 / 3 / 4 / 4
Ease to make (1): 5 / 3 / 3 / 2
No table fixing (2): 5 / 5 / 5 / 1
Totals: Idea 1: 49, Idea 2: 37, Idea 3: 52, Idea 4: 29
Idea 3 scored highest.

SLIDE 16 - CHOSEN DESIGN AND JUSTIFICATION
Chosen: Idea 3 with changes from feedback. I showed a cardboard model to Mrs Okonkwo on 14 March. She liked it but asked that the lid is not removed too easily by students. So I added a tab and notch at the lid end so it slides only one way.
Why it meets the specification:
- Hides the lead so cables are neat (spec 3) - the lead sits in a recess 34 cm long
- Weight of the plywood box, about 600 g with lead, plus 4 rubber feet stops sliding (spec 3)
- 5 slots, 9 mm wide, meets spec 2; phone slots 15 mm meets spec 1
- Size 38 x 12 x 8 cm meets spec 4
- Plywood sheet costs about 5 pounds for the amount needed (spec 5)
Final sketch: top, front and side views with dimensions (see annotations: lid 38 x 12, thickness 6 mm, side walls 8 cm, corner radius 4 mm)

SLIDE 17 - PLANNING DETAILS
Materials: 6 mm birch ply, one 60 x 30 cm sheet; PVA glue; clear varnish; 4 rubber feet
Tools: laser cutter, sandpaper (240 grit), clamps, brush
Lesson 1: draw in CAD (Tinkercad/Illustrator), check measurements against the lead, export file
Lesson 2: laser cut the 6 parts, test fit with cardboard first
Lesson 3: sand, glue with clamps, leave 24 hours to dry
Lesson 4: varnish 2 coats, fit feet, test
Safety: use the laser cutter only with the teacher present and extraction on, wear a mask when sanding, ventilate for varnish
Risks: wrong size of recess (solved by a cardboard test), wood warping (use clamps flat)
Time plan: 4 lessons plus 24 hours of drying and 2 hours of varnish drying

task: Design folio part 1: identify a need and a client, research and analyse the need, existing products and a design brief (criterion A). Then write a specification, develop a range of feasible design ideas, choose and justify one design and show planning details (criterion B).
text:
DESIGN PROJECT - DESK ORGANISER
Name: Year 10 Design
Criteria A and B

THE PROBLEM
My younger brother Omar is 9 years old and his desk is always messy. He has pens, pencils, rulers, rubbers and stationery everywhere and he can never find things. This makes him late for school sometimes and it makes him upset. My mum says it is a mess. I want to design a desk organiser to help him.

Caption: photo of Omar's messy desk

CLIENT
My client is Omar, my brother. He is 9. He likes football and Minecraft. I asked him what he wants and he said "something cool for my pens". My mum also said it should be strong and not break.

WHY THIS IS A GOOD PROBLEM
Lots of people have messy desks so a good organiser could help many people. A tidy desk helps you concentrate and do better in school. Organisers are sold in many shops.

RESEARCH PLAN
- Look at organisers online
- Ask Omar what he wants
- Find out about materials
- Look at what is popular
- Think about colours and the style

RESEARCH
I went on the internet to find desk organisers. There are a lot of different organisers. Some are made of plastic and some are made of wood, metal or cardboard. Plastic is cheap and light and it comes in many colours. Wood is stronger and looks nice but it costs more. Metal organisers are made of mesh and they last a long time. Cardboard is cheap but it breaks easily.

Desk organisers have been around for many years. People used them in offices to keep paper and pens. They are now used in homes and schools also. Many are made in factories in China and sold in shops like IKEA and WHSmith.

I asked Omar some questions:
What do you want on your desk? pens, pencils, rubbers, a sharpener, a ruler
What colours do you like? blue and green
Do you want a football design? yes
Do you want it to be big or small? medium

EXISTING PRODUCTS
Product 1 - IKEA mesh organiser. It is made of metal and has 3 compartments. It looks good. It costs 5 pounds. It is quite plain and I think Omar would find it boring.
Product 2 - Plastic pen pot with football design. It is cheap and it has a football on it. But it only holds pens and it is small.
Product 3 - Wooden organiser with drawers. It is nice and strong and has lots of places for things. It is expensive, about 20 pounds.
Product 4 - Cardboard organiser. It is cheap but it isn't strong and looks bad.
Comparing them, I like the wooden one the best because it is strong and has lots of storage. The plastic one is good for Omar because of the football.

DESIGN BRIEF
I will design and make a desk organiser for my brother Omar. It should be strong, look good and have places for his pens, pencils and rubber. It should be a football theme.

SPECIFICATION
- It must look cool
- It must be strong
- It must be easy to use
- It should be the right size for his desk
- It should be made from good materials
- It must be safe
- It should be colourful
- It should not cost too much
- It should have enough space for his stationery
- It should be attractive and Omar must like it

IDEA 1
A pen pot shaped like a football. Made of plastic. It has hexagon pattern in black and white. Holds pens only.
Good: looks like a football, simple
Bad: only holds pens

IDEA 2
Wooden box with 3 sections. Painted green like a football pitch with white lines. Pens in one section, rubbers in another, rulers in the third.
Good: holds many things, looks like a pitch
Bad: might take a long time to make

IDEA 3
A football goal organiser. The goal frame is made of wood and there are small shelves inside it for things. The pens go in a hole at the top.
Good: fun idea
Bad: not sure if strong

IDEA 4
A cylinder organiser with different sizes. Made out of cardboard tubes that are painted.
Good: cheap
Bad: not strong

IDEA 5
A tiered organiser with 2 levels, in blue plastic.
Good: lots of space
Bad: boring

CHOOSING MY DESIGN
I chose Idea 2, the wooden box with 3 sections like a football pitch. I chose it because it is strong, it can hold lots of stuff and it is a football theme which Omar will like. It is also easy to make because it is a box. Also I like wood because it is a good material and it looks good. I think Omar will like it a lot.

Final design: drawing of the box with sections, measurements 25 cm long, 12 cm wide, 8 cm high.

PLANNING
Materials: wood, glue, paint
Tools: saw, hammer, sandpaper, paintbrush
Steps:
1. Measure and mark the wood
2. Cut the wood
3. Sand it
4. Glue the pieces together
5. Paint it green with white lines
6. Let it dry
Time: about 3 weeks.
Safety: be careful with the saw and wear goggles.

CONCLUSION
I think my design is good and will solve the problem. Omar will have a tidy desk and he will be happy. I have done lots of research and I have made a good plan, so I think my organiser will be a success. I am excited to start making it.

Design Folio - Phone Stand

SLIDE 1 - THE PROBLEM
People hold their phones for a long time and their hands get tired. When you watch videos or look at recipes the phone falls over. A phone stand will help with this problem. This is a big problem for lots of people because everyone has a phone these days.

SLIDE 2 - CLIENT
My client is my friend Jake. He has a phone and he likes watching videos. He said he would like a stand. I asked him what he wanted and he said he wanted something good.

SLIDE 3 - RESEARCH
Phone stands are used to hold phones. They can be made of plastic, wood or metal. You can buy them in shops and online. People like them because they are useful. Phones are used for calling, texting, watching videos, playing games and taking photos. Phones were invented a long time ago and now they are smartphones. Phone stands are also called phone holders or phone docks. Some of them can be used in cars.

I looked at the internet and I found phone stands in different colours. Some are cheap and some are expensive. Some are for desks and some are for beds. Some can fold. Lots of people have them and they are popular. I think this means they are a good product to make.

SLIDE 4 - EXISTING PRODUCT
I found one phone stand online. It is black and made of plastic. It costs 5 pounds. It is good because it holds the phone and it looks nice. It is not so good because it is plain. I would like to make mine look better than this one.

SLIDE 5 - DESIGN BRIEF
Make a phone stand for Jake that is good.

SLIDE 6 - SPECIFICATION
It should be good, strong and look nice. It should hold a phone. It should be the right size. It should not be too expensive.

SLIDE 7 - IDEAS
Idea 1: a stand made of wood with a slot (sketch of a block with a line)
Idea 2: a stand made of plastic with a slot (same sketch)
Idea 3: a stand made of cardboard
Idea 4: a stand made of metal

SLIDE 8 - CHOICE
I chose idea 1 because it is the best one and it looks good. Wood is a good material because it is strong and I can use it in school. I think Jake will like it. The other ideas were not as good as this one.

SLIDE 9 - PLAN
Get wood
Cut the wood
Make the slot
Sand it
Paint it
Give it to Jake
Time: 3 lessons

SLIDE 10 - CONCLUSION
I think my phone stand will be good. I have done lots of research and I am happy with my idea. I think Jake will like it.

task: Design folio part 2: make your chosen solution following a plan, explaining changes made (criterion C). Then test the solution, evaluate it against your specification, suggest improvements and explain its impact (criterion D).
text:
Making the library charging station

Plan for making

Before I started making I rewrote my plan from criterion B as a step table with times, so that I could check progress each lesson. Lesson 1 (50 min): finish CAD of six parts and test-print the layout on cardboard. Lesson 2: laser cut the plywood. Lesson 3: sand and dry fit, then glue. Lesson 4: varnish and fit rubber feet. I also listed the order for gluing, because the recess had to be assembled before the lid rails were fitted and I knew that it would be hard to reach inside afterwards. The safety plan was that the laser cutter was used only with Mr Davies present and with the extraction fan on, that I wore a dust mask for sanding, and that I varnished in the ventilated prep room away from other students.

How I made it

In lesson 1 I drew the base (38 x 12 cm), two long walls, two end walls and a lid in Illustrator. When I laid the cardboard test pieces on the extension lead I found my recess was only 33.5 cm long, but the lead is 33 cm plus a 2 cm plug lump at the end. The lead would not have fitted. Change 1: I lengthened the inside recess to 36 cm, which made the whole box 40 cm. This broke my specification point 4 (footprint no bigger than 40 x 15), but only just, as 40 is the maximum, so I accepted it. I reduced the end walls from 8 mm to 6 mm to keep it at exactly 40 cm.

In lesson 2 the laser cut the pieces in about 12 minutes. I saw that the first piece had burn marks along the edges and the 9 mm cable slots were charred. I increased the speed from 20 to 30 and reduced power from 70 to 55 percent on the second attempt, which gave much cleaner edges. That cost me one extra sheet of ply (60p) and about 10 minutes, but it was worth it because the slots had to be smooth to avoid damaging cables.

Lesson 3 was the sanding and gluing. I sanded the slot edges using 240 grit paper wrapped round a pencil so that the inside of the slots was rounded. I glued the walls to the base with PVA and checked square corners with a set square, then clamped them. At this stage I noticed that the lid did not slide because the wood had expanded a little after the laser. Change 2: I sanded the lid rails by 0.5 mm, testing after each pass, until the lid slid smoothly but was not loose.

In lesson 4 I applied two coats of clear varnish, leaving 30 minutes between coats, and fitted 4 rubber feet to the base. I also added the tab and notch that the client asked for so that the lid can be removed only by sliding it one way. That meant gluing a 5 mm ply strip, which I had not planned, but it only took five minutes. In total I took one extra half lesson at lunchtime to finish, since the sanding took longer than I estimated (I had said 20 minutes and it took 40).

Skills used: CAD drawing, laser cutting, accurate sanding, clamping and gluing, finishing. I was careful to follow the plan but I kept a log with photographs after every stage so I could show what I changed and why.

Testing the solution

I tested my station against each point of the specification.
1. Three phones upright: I tested with an iPhone 13 with case (11 mm), a Samsung A14 (9 mm) and a thicker rugged case (13 mm). All three stood upright. PASS.
2. Cable slots: 5 slots measured with callipers at 9.0, 9.1, 9.0, 9.2 and 9.0 mm. USB-C, Lightning and laptop chargers (7 mm) all passed through. PASS.
3. Holding the lead: I attached a spring balance to a cable and pulled horizontally. The station slid at about 6 N, so it passed the target of 5 N but with only a small margin. PASS, narrowly.
4. Footprint: 40.0 x 12.5 x 8 cm. PASS (just).
5. Cost: plywood 5.00 pounds, feet 1.20, glue and varnish from school stock, an extra sheet 0.60. Total 6.80, under 8 pounds. PASS.
6. Wipe test: I dropped juice on it and wiped with a cloth, which cleaned the varnished top, but the juice left a slight stain in the raw end grain. PARTLY.
7. Sharp edges: all corners rounded with a 4 mm radius, checked by two classmates. PASS.
8. No fixing to the table and ventilation: the lead has its air gaps uncovered because the lid has 2 mm gaps at the sides. PASS.
9. Made in 4 lessons: I used 4.5. PARTLY.

I also got feedback from Mrs Okonkwo and from 5 students who used it for a week at table 4. Mrs Okonkwo said it was "neat and stable". Three students said that the phone slots were good but two said the gap between slots was too narrow to put a charger plug in the next to a phone.

Evaluation

Overall the product meets 7 of 9 specification points fully and the other two partly. It solves the main problem since cables don't tangle and phones aren't on the floor. In the week trial no cable was pulled out of the lead at table 4 and no phone fell, compared with the 2 and 3 incidents I observed before, although that is a small sample from one table in one week.

The weaknesses are: the sliding force of 6 N is marginal. If a student pulls a cable hard the box moves. I think that adding a thin cork or rubber strip to the base or more weight (a 3 mm steel plate inside) would help. The end grain absorbed liquid, so it should be sealed with three coats or use a sealing wax. The slots are too close together for chargers with a large plug, so the spacing should be 25 mm not 18 mm, though this would make the box 4 cm longer and break the footprint, so I would need to stagger them.

Improvements: (1) bigger rubber feet or anti-slip pads; (2) a third coat of varnish on cut edges; (3) staggered slots; (4) a handle cut-out for carrying. If I made it again I would test the lead fit with the real extension lead before cutting.

Impact

For the client, the product removes the trip hazard that she worried about and costs 6.80 pounds each, so six could be made for about 41 pounds, within her budget. For users, it is a small change but it keeps phones safer. The material is plywood, a renewable resource, and I used only one sheet and a spare, with offcuts left to reuse, so the environmental impact is limited. However, because the station only holds a power strip, it encourages students to keep using more electricity at school, and if it was mass-produced it would be better to use recycled wood fibre or recycled plastic. There is also a social impact because tidier tables make the library safer and calmer for everyone, including students with mobility needs who could be at risk from loose cables on the floor.

task: Design folio part 2: make your chosen solution following a plan, explaining changes made (criterion C). Then test the solution, evaluate it against your specification, suggest improvements and explain its impact (criterion D).
text:
Making and evaluating my desk organiser

Making

I made my desk organiser in the workshop over about 5 lessons. First I got the wood. I used a piece of pine that was 25 cm long and I cut it into pieces with the saw. I had to cut the base, the sides and the dividers. It was hard to cut straight lines but I tried my best. Then I sanded the pieces with sandpaper to make them smooth. After that I glued the sides to the base and put the dividers in to make the three sections. I waited for the glue to dry for one lesson. Then I painted it green with white lines like a football pitch. I used acrylic paint and I put two coats. I painted a white circle in the middle and I put a small football on one end.

I followed my plan most of the time. I changed some things when I was making it. The first change was that I used pine instead of a different kind of wood because it was easy to find. I also made the box a bit shorter because I had less wood than I thought. The second change was that I made the dividers thinner because the first ones were too thick. The third change was that I didn't use the nails because the glue was good enough. I think these changes were fine.

I used a saw, sandpaper, glue, clamps and paintbrushes. I used the safety goggles when I was sawing and I tied my hair back. I kept my work space clean. My teacher helped me with the sawing at the start. It took me a bit longer than I planned because the glue took time to dry and I made a mistake with the first divider so I had to cut a new one. I think the quality of my making is quite good but the corners are not perfectly square and there is a small gap on one side where the glue squeezed out.

Testing

To test my organiser I put Omar's stationery in it. I put 6 pens in one section, the rubber and sharpener in the second and the ruler and pencils in the third. Everything fitted. I also tested it by pushing it and by dropping it from the desk and it did not break. It was strong. I showed it to Omar and he said it was "cool" and he liked the football pitch. My mum also said she liked it and it looks neat.

I asked Omar to use it for a week. He used it every day and his desk was tidier than before. He said he could find his things more easily. Once he knocked it off the desk but it did not break.

Evaluation

I think my organiser was successful. It met my specification because it looks cool, it is strong, it is easy to use, it is the right size for the desk, and it has enough space for the stationery. It was also not expensive because I used wood from school. It is safe because I sanded it so there are no splinters. The colours are good, and the football theme makes it fun, so Omar likes it. I am very pleased with the result.

Some things were not so good. The painting was a bit messy, the lines are not straight, and there is a gap on one side. The pens are a bit loose in the section and the box is a bit heavy. If I made it again I would make it neater and more careful. I could also use a different wood or maybe plastic.

How I could improve it

To improve it I could add a drawer for small things like paper clips. I could also add a lid. I could make it in different colours, for example blue like the sky. I could use better paint so it does not scratch. I could add rubber feet so that it doesn't scratch the desk. I could also make the sections different sizes.

Impact

My organiser has a good impact on Omar because he is happier and he has a tidy desk. It could also have an impact on other people because they might want one too. Wood is a natural material so it is good for the environment, but cutting down trees is bad so we should be careful. I used paint that is water based so it is not so bad for the environment. In the future people might want organisers made of recycled materials.

In conclusion, I think that my project went well. I learned how to use tools and how to make something from start to finish. I am proud of my organiser and Omar is happy with it. It was a great project and I enjoyed making it. I would like to do more projects like this in the future.

task: Design folio part 1: identify a need and a client, research and analyse the need, existing products and a design brief (criterion A). Then write a specification, develop a range of feasible design ideas, choose and justify one design and show planning details (criterion B).
text:
Design folio: a backpack for school

Introduction

For my design project I have decided to design a backpack. A backpack is a bag that is carried on the back, and it is used by millions of students all around the world every day. I chose a backpack because I use one every day and I think it is a very important product. In this folio I will write about the history of backpacks, the different types, and what I like.

The history of the backpack

The history of the backpack goes back thousands of years. The earliest known backpack-like carrying device was found with Otzi the Iceman, a man who lived about 5,300 years ago in the Alps and whose frozen body was discovered in 1991. He carried a frame made of hazel wood with a bag attached to it. Throughout history, people have always needed a way to carry their belongings, and soldiers, travellers and hunters all used some kind of pack. In ancient times people used animal skins, woven grass and cloth to carry goods on their backs. Roman soldiers carried a pack on a stick called a sarcina, which held their food, tools and clothing on long marches.

During the Middle Ages, pilgrims and peasants carried bundles on their backs, often made from cloth tied with rope. As exploration grew in the 16th and 17th centuries, explorers and sailors used canvas and leather bags to carry supplies. In the 19th century, armies began to use knapsacks made of canvas and leather. These were uncomfortable because the weight was carried on the shoulders and had no support.

The modern backpack began to develop in the early 20th century. In 1908 Ole F. Bergan, a Norwegian inventor, designed the first rucksack with a wooden frame, and he called it the Bergans rucksack. In the 1920s, Lloyd F. Nelson developed a frame backpack made of bamboo. In 1938 Gerry Cunningham made the first backpack with a zip, and in the 1950s Dick Kelty developed aluminium frame packs that were lighter and stronger. Nylon was introduced during the Second World War and this made the packs lighter and water resistant. In the 1960s and 1970s, backpacks became popular with hikers and young people, and companies such as The North Face, Jansport, Eastpak and Osprey started to make them for everyday use. In the 1980s and 1990s, the backpack became the standard bag for students, with brands like Nike, Adidas and Herschel producing fashionable versions. Today, backpacks come in many shapes, sizes and materials, from small fashion bags to large travel packs and laptop bags with USB ports and anti-theft features.

Types of backpacks

There are many different types of backpacks. Hiking backpacks are large and designed for carrying heavy loads over long distances. They have padded straps, a hip belt and a frame. Daypacks are smaller and used for short trips. School backpacks are used to carry books, stationery and lunch. Laptop backpacks have a padded compartment to protect electronics. Travel backpacks open like a suitcase. Drawstring bags are simple and light and are often used for PE kit. Sling bags have one strap and are worn across the body. Roll top backpacks are waterproof and closed by rolling the top. There are also fashion backpacks, which are designed to look good and come in different colours, and they are made of leather, canvas or nylon.

Materials used in backpacks

Backpacks can be made from different materials. Nylon is very popular because it is strong, light and water resistant. Polyester is also used and it is cheaper. Canvas is a heavy cotton fabric which is strong but not waterproof. Leather looks good and lasts a long time but is heavy and expensive. Recycled materials such as recycled PET plastic bottles are now used by some brands to reduce the impact on the environment. Zips are made from plastic or metal, and straps are made from webbing and foam.

Why backpacks are important

Backpacks are important because they let us carry things easily and keep our hands free. Using two straps spreads the weight across both shoulders, which is better for the back than using a shoulder bag. Doctors say that a backpack should weigh no more than 10 to 15 percent of body weight. Heavy backpacks can cause back pain, so it is important to wear them correctly. Backpacks are an important part of student life and fashion. They are also a big industry, with millions sold each year around the world.

Things I like

I like a lot of things in a backpack. I like it to be black because black goes with everything. I like lots of pockets. I like it to have a place for my water bottle. I like it to be comfortable. I like it to look cool and fashionable. I like a bag that has a good brand name, such as Nike. I like a bag that has a laptop pocket. I like it to have a place for headphones. I like zips that are smooth. I like it when the straps are padded. I like a bag that is not too heavy. I like a logo on the front. I like a bag that is waterproof because it rains a lot. I like it to be big enough for all my books. I like when there are lots of colours. I like a bag that lasts for a long time. I like it to be easy to clean.

Who uses backpacks

Lots of people use backpacks. Students use them for school. Workers use them for carrying laptops. Hikers use them for camping. Tourists use them for travelling. Children use them for nursery. Soldiers use them in the army. Cyclists use them too. I think that everybody uses backpacks at some time in their life, and that is why it is a good thing to design.

Design brief

I will design a backpack that is good for school and that I will like. It will be comfortable and look good and have a lot of space.

Specification

My backpack should be comfortable, have lots of pockets, look good, be strong, be waterproof, be black, and be the right size. It should have a place for a water bottle and a laptop.

My idea

My idea is to design a black backpack with a lot of pockets, a laptop pocket, and a water bottle pocket. It will be made from nylon and it will have padded straps and a logo on the front. I think this will be a very good design because it has everything that I like.

Planning

I will get the materials, cut the fabric, sew the pieces, add the zips and the straps. I will finish it in a few weeks.

Conclusion

In conclusion, backpacks have a long and interesting history and are very important in our lives. I have learned a lot about backpacks and I think that I will make a great backpack. I really enjoy design and I am looking forward to making my backpack.
